summary: Explains how a device finds the right Location Information Server (LIS) in its local access network. It defines DHCP options for IPv4 and IPv6 that carry a domain name, which is then resolved through DNS to locate the server. The location itself is then requested from that server with a separate protocol.

plainLanguage.summary:
A device that wants to know where it is needs to find the right server to ask. This RFC explains how it finds that server, using the network's own configuration service and the DNS.

The result is the address of a location server, which the device then checks before relying on it.

subtitle: How a device finds the server that knows where it is, using DHCP and the DNS.

tldr.problem: A device that wants to know its own location has to ask a Location Information Server, but the right server depends on the access network the device is attached to, and that changes when the device moves.
tldr.mechanism: The access network gives the device a domain name in a new DHCP option, and the device resolves that name with URI-enabled NAPTR using the LIS and HELD tags to get an HTTP or HTTPS URI for the server.
tldr.outcome: The device ends up with a URI it can use to ask for its location, and it checks the server before trusting it. The document is a Proposed Standard and the URI is only for use with HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery.

today: RFC 5986 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines how a device finds a location information server, and the URI it produces is meant to be used with HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery, defined in RFC 5985.

sections.title: Why a Device Has to Find Its Location Server
sections.content:
The location of a device is a useful and sometimes necessary part of many services. A Location Information Server (LIS) provides that location information to devices that are attached to access networks used for Internet access. The LIS uses knowledge of the access network and its physical topology to generate and serve location information.

Each access network needs specific knowledge about its topology, so it is important to discover the LIS that holds that knowledge, the one that serves the current access network. Automatic discovery matters whenever there is any chance of the device moving outside a single access network. Reliance on static configuration can lead to unexpected errors when a device moves between access networks.

This document describes a process a device can use to discover a LIS. It uses a DHCP option and the DNS. The product of the process is an HTTP or HTTPS URI that identifies a LIS.

That URI is suitable for location configuration only. The device MUST dereference it using the process described in HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD), RFC 5985. URIs discovered this way are not location URIs, and dereferencing one of them gives the location of the requestor only. Devices MUST NOT embed these URIs in fields of other protocols that carry the location of the device.
sections.plainLanguage: A device that wants to know where it is needs to find the right server to ask. This RFC explains how it finds that server, using the network's own configuration service and the DNS.

sections.title: The Discovery Procedure in Outline
sections.content:
DHCP is a commonly used mechanism for providing the bootstrap configuration that lets a device operate in a particular network. The configuration it carries is largely static: it does not change while the device is attached. Physical location information may change over that time, but the address of the LIS does not. That is why DHCP suits the job of telling a device the address of a LIS.

The document defines a DHCP option that produces a domain name identifying the local access network, in Section 3. Section 4 describes a method that uses URI-enabled NAPTR, a profile of the Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service, to produce a URI for the LIS, and the input to that method is the DHCP option.

For that discovery profile, an Application Service tag "LIS" and an Application Protocol tag "HELD" have been created and registered with IANA. Given the domain name, the NAPTR records use the two tags to find a URI for a LIS that supports the HELD protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Two standard pieces do the work: the network's DHCP server names the access network, and the DNS turns that name into the address of the location server.

sections.title: The Discovery Procedure
sections.content:
A device with several network interfaces could be served by a different access network on each, with a different LIS for each. The device SHOULD try to discover the LIS for each interface, stopping when one is found successfully on any interface.

The procedure has three steps. First, acquire the access network domain name, which might be repeated for each interface; domain names from other sources might also be added. Second, apply U-NAPTR resolution to each of those domain names to discover a LIS URI. Third, verify that the LIS is able to provide location information; the first URI that produces a successful response is used.

A device MUST support discovery using the access network domain name DHCP option as input to U-NAPTR resolution. If that option is not available, DHCPv4 option 15 is used. Other domain names MAY be used.

After discovering a URI, the device MUST try to verify that the LIS can provide location information. For HELD it makes a location request to the LIS, and any HTTP 200 response containing a HELD response means success, including HELD error responses, with the exception of the notLocatable error. If the LIS ever replies with notLocatable, the device MUST continue or restart the discovery process, and SHOULD NOT make further requests to that LIS until its network attachment changes or it finds a LIS on another interface.

Static configuration of a domain name or a LIS URI MAY be used, but if the device has moved from its usual location, static configuration might point at a LIS that cannot give accurate location information.

Two situations need care. A residential gateway sits between the device and the access network in a fixed wireline environment, and if it does not give the right information to the devices it serves, those devices cannot discover a LIS. A gateway can help by passing on a domain name it got from the access network provider, by discovering a LIS on its own external interface and passing on the name that worked, by including configuration that names a particular LIS, or by acting as a LIS itself. A gateway that relies on configuration rather than discovery gives wrong answers if it is moved. And a device MUST NOT attempt discovery over a VPN interface until it has tried and failed on all other non-VPN interfaces, because a LIS found that way is unlikely to hold the information needed for an accurate location.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks for the name of the access network, turns that name into the address of a location server with the DNS, and then checks that the server answers. If the server says it cannot locate the device, the device starts again with another name or another interface.

sections.title: The DHCP Options That Carry the Domain Name
sections.content:
DHCP gives the access network provider a direct way to configure a device. The access network domain name option identifies a domain name that is suitable for service discovery inside the access network, and that name is the input to the U-NAPTR resolution for LIS discovery. The name is owned by the access network operator and is meant for finding services inside that access network. This document registers a DHCP option for it, for both IPv4 and IPv6.

The domain name is encoded as in Section 3.1 of RFC 1035. Each label is a one-octet length field followed by that number of octets, and since every domain name ends with the null label of the root, the name is terminated by a length byte of zero. The high-order two bits of every length octet MUST be zero, and the remaining six bits limit a label to 63 octets or less. To keep implementations simple, the total length of a domain name, counting the label octets and the length octets, is restricted to 255 octets or less. The example "example.com." is encoded in 13 octets.

The DHCPv4 option has the option code OPTION_V4_ACCESS_DOMAIN, 213, and a length field giving the length of the whole option in octets. The option value is the domain name. A DHCPv4 client MAY ask for the option in a Parameter Request List. The option carries a single domain name, so it MUST contain precisely one root label.

The DHCPv6 option is formatted the same way, with the option code OPTION_V6_ACCESS_DOMAIN, 57. A DHCPv6 client MAY ask for it in an Options Request Option, and it too MUST contain precisely one root label.

Other domain names may be known to the device, and it MAY repeat the U-NAPTR process with them. DHCPv4 option 15 gives an indication of the domain name the host uses for resolving hostnames, and is used when the DHCPv4 access domain name option is not available. But alternative domain names MUST NOT be used unless the access network domain name option is unsuccessful, or unless outside information says a particular name is to be used. A DHCP server may offer other names, for example from the fully qualified domain name options of RFC 4702 and RFC 4704, but those are given without any thought of LIS discovery, so they are unlikely to hold useful values.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP carries the domain name of the access network. The name is written in the usual DNS form, with a length byte in front of each label, and the same option exists for IPv4 and IPv6.

sections.title: U-NAPTR Resolution of a LIS URI
sections.content:
U-NAPTR resolution takes a domain name as input and produces a URI that identifies the LIS. It also needs an Application Service tag and an Application Protocol tag, which tell LIS-related NAPTR records apart from other records for that domain. The Application Service tag "LIS" identifies the location service for a domain, and the Application Protocol tag "HELD" identifies a LIS that understands the HELD protocol.

The RFC gives example NAPTR records. Iterative NAPTR resolution delegates responsibility for the LIS service from zonea.example.net and zoneb.example.net to outsource.example.com, and the final record there carries a regular expression that produces the URI https://lis.example.org:4802/?c=ex.

One iteration of the algorithm can produce several results, and the order and preference values in the NAPTR record decide which one is used. A device MAY try the alternatives if the first choice does not work, but if a request to the resulting URI produces a HELD notLocatable response, the device SHOULD NOT try any alternative from the same domain name.

An HTTPS LIS URI that is the product of U-NAPTR MUST be authenticated using the domain name method of Section 3.1 of RFC 2818. The domain name used for that authentication is the one taken from the URI, not the one that was the input to the resolution.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS holds records that say where the location server is for a given name. The records carry two tags, one for the service and one for the protocol, so that only the location records are picked out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The address of a LIS is usually well known inside an access network, so intercepting messages does not raise particular concerns. The main attack is impersonation of a LIS. The LIS provides location information, that information matters to a number of network services, and a device does not necessarily have a prior relationship with a LIS. The methods described in the document limit the probability of such an attack or give some protection against it, and they MUST be applied unless similar protections are in place, or in cases such as an emergency where location information of dubious origin is arguably better than none.

An attacker could try to compromise discovery at three stages: by providing a falsified domain name to use as input to U-NAPTR, by altering the DNS records used in the resolution, or by impersonating the LIS.

The domain name used to authenticate the LIS is the input to the U-NAPTR process, not its output, so the results of DNS queries do not need integrity protection. An HTTPS URI is authenticated with the method of Section 3.1 of RFC 2818. HTTP client implementations often cannot authenticate a name other than the one in the request URI, which is the U-NAPTR output, so a client MAY reject URIs whose domain name differs from the U-NAPTR input. To support such endpoints, network administrators SHOULD make sure that the domain name in the DHCP option is the same as the one in the resulting URI.

Authentication of the LIS relies on the integrity of the domain name acquired from DHCP, so an attacker who can falsify that name defeats the protection. Preventing DHCP messages from being modified or spoofed is therefore necessary, and link-layer security is commonly used for that. DHCP authentication may also help. A LIS identified by an HTTP URI cannot be authenticated at all, and unsecured HTTP does not meet the HELD requirements for confidentiality and integrity, so a device is exposed to several attacks in that case. Lower-layer protections, such as Layer 2 traffic separation, may be used instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk is that someone pretends to be the location server and gives a wrong answer. The protection is to check the server's name against the name the network gave the device, which is why the name has to arrive intact.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has assigned option code 213 for the DHCPv4 option that carries an access network domain name, and option code 57 for the DHCPv6 option.

The document also registers a new S-NAPTR and U-NAPTR Application Service tag, LIS, whose intended usage is to identify a service that provides a device with its location information, and a new Application Protocol tag, HELD, whose intended usage is to identify the HELD protocol. The HELD tag applies to the LIS service tag, and its terminal NAPTR record type is U.
sections.plainLanguage: The option numbers and the two DNS tags were registered so that every implementation uses the same values.
